newsitem.title: USA: Aetna down on Q2, HMO growth prospects.
newsitem.headline: Aetna down on Q2, HMO growth prospects.

text.p: Shares of Aetna Inc, one of the country's largest health insurers, fell more than 10 percent Tuesday afternoon after the company reported disappointing second-quarter earnings and scaled back growth prospects for the year.

Aetna said it was trimming the outlook for commercial HMO and Medicare enrollment growth in 1997 to the 10-11 percent range from a previous 13-15 percent range as it resists cutting prices to attract business.
Commercial HMO enrollment grew by 10 percent in the second quarter, but that fell short of analysts' expectations.
The Hartford, Conn.-based company's second-quarter health insurance results also were hurt by an increase in commercial HMO and Medicare medical costs, analysts said.
"Medical costs were a little higher, pricing was at the low end of prior indications and enrollment was at the low end," Salomon analyst Robert Hoehn said.
Aetna's second quarter operating earnings also included a $31 million contribution from a reduction in a reserve.

Aetna reported second-quarter operating earnings of $1.27 a share. But excluding that special contribution, second-quarter operating earnings were really about $1.15 a share, analysts said, about $0.12 short of analysts' First Call consensus estimate.

Aetna shares fell 14-5/16, or about 12 percent, to 102-3/4 in mid-afternoon trading. The shares of other HMOs also moved lower. Oxford Health Plans Inc fell four, or nearly five percent, to 81-11/16; United HealthCare Corp fell 4-2/16, or about four percent, to 57-1/4; and Humana Inc fell 3/8, or about 1.5 percent, to 24.
"The most important thing is that they reduced their growth outlook in terms of membership growth for the HMOs," Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman said.
"The biggest thing is concern about the growth outlook," he said. "This is supposed to be a growth stock in a growth business."

Meanwhile, operating earnings from Aetna U.S. Healthcare's Health Risk business, which includes those products in which the company assumes all or a majority of health care cost and utilization risk, decreased from a year ago on a pro forma basis.
Results for the Health Risk business were pressured by increases in medical costs, Aetna said.
But Merrill Lynch analyst Margo Vignola told the firm's salesforce that she believes the medical cost problems should abate in coming months, a market source said.
Instead, she recommended investors use the current drop in the price of the stock as a buying opportunity.
In addition, she expects pricing to improve in the second half of the year, the source said.
Aetna also did a good job in cutting costs in the second quarter, Standard & Poor's director Arun Kumar said.

Kumar, head of the health insurance group at Standard & Poor's said Aetna's cost-cutting measures have helped to bolster his confidence in the company's ability to integrate U.S. Healthcare, which it acquired last year.

Indeed, he said, Standard & Poor's last week raised Aetna's claims-paying ability rating because of the company's excellent earnings and excellent business profile in the health insurance and managed care markets.
But, he said, if enrollment growth doesn't improve next year, he said, that "might put up a red flag."
"That will point to problems, that the business itself is not growing," he said.
